query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled pre-oxidation treatment that forms a continuous, low-defect Al2O3/Cr-rich passivating oxide film on the as-built alloy surface will act as an effective diffusion barrier to oxygen ingress, thereby mitigating internal oxidation and catastrophic failure during high-temperature exposure.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy with a native, thin, and inhomogeneous oxide layer and inherent surface defects.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled low‐temperature pre‐oxidation treatment (e.g., heat at 650 °C for 10 h in a controlled O2 atmosphere) to form a well-adherent, continuous oxide film before high‐temperature exposure.
generation.conditions: Pre‐oxidation at 650 °C for 10 h under controlled oxygen partial pressure, followed by oxidation exposure at 850 °C for 100 h in air.
generation.structural_mediator: The pre‐formed oxide film with low defect density provides an effective barrier to oxygen diffusion, curtailing the onset of internal oxidation.
generation.mechanism: A continuous, pre‐formed oxide scale minimizes discontinuities and defects that act as fast diffusion paths for oxygen. This barrier reduces oxygen ingress during subsequent high‐temperature exposure, thereby slowing internal oxidation and delaying catastrophic structural degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Pre‐oxidized samples will display a lower cumulative mass gain, a more uniform and adherent oxide layer, and reduced internal oxidation compared to samples without pre‐oxidation treatment.
generation.baseline: As‐built samples with a native thin and heterogeneous oxide layer quickly develop discontinuous oxide scales and internal oxidation under high‐temperature conditions, leading to earlier failure.
generation.boundary: This mechanism applies for pre‐oxidation treatments at moderate temperatures (~650 °C) followed by high‐temperature exposure (~850 °C) for durations around 100 h; deviations in temperature or oxygen partial pressure may affect oxide scale formation.
generation.uncertainty: The pre‐oxidation treatment parameters (time and temperature) must be carefully optimized; there is uncertainty regarding the long‐term stability of the pre‐formed oxide film at 850 °C.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of samples: one group receives the pre‐oxidation treatment (650 °C for 10 h in controlled O2) and the other remains untreated. Then expose both groups to 850 °C for 100 h in air and assess oxide scale quality and internal oxidation.
measurements: SEM/TEM imaging of oxide scale morphology and continuity
XRD analysis for phase identification in the oxide layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre‐oxidized samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in oxide film continuity, reduced oxygen ingress, and lower mass gain compared to untreated samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Al seems to have a minor effect on both Ni and Co, both of which are the weakest oxidizing component and it seems to have no effects on both unoxidized and oxidized states. We infer that Al addition does not have significant electronic interaction with Co and Ni (Fig. 4h, i), this is shown as their oxidation behavior remains the same in Fig. 4d. Figure 4j summarizes these interactions where Mn-Al tends to have the strongest interaction and both Ni and Co being the weakest. This study uncovers the oxidation process in compositionally complex alloys. Our study involved subjecting an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy to oxidation at 400 °C under 10 mbar oxygen pressure for both ex situ and in situ observations. Ex situ observations, conducted using TEM after 120 min of oxidation, revealed a layered oxide structure. The 20 nm oxide layer on the equiatomic base alloy exhibited a composition sequence of Ni-rich (bottom layer), Cr-rich, and then Fe, Mn, and Co-rich layers (outer oxide). We chose a relatively low oxidation temperature to prevent phase transformation in the alloy, focusing solely on examining the oxidation process in the super-saturated alloy condition. This refined structure enhances oxygen-blocking efficiency and thermal stress resistance by mitigating interfacial defects and optimizing thermal expansion matching. The grain boundary pinning effect of Y not only refines ZrO2 grains but also establishes dynamic equilibrium between suppressed cation diffusion (Cr3+) and regulated anion transport (O2−), synergistically optimizing elemental migration resistance, scale densification, and interfacial stability. Under these mechanisms, the 2.0 wt.% Y2O3 coating achieves a 52% reduction in oxidation-induced mass gain (8.749 mg/cm2) compared to undoped systems, demonstrating optimal high-temperature protective performance. Figure 15 depicts the oxidation mechanisms of FeCrAl coatings. Excessive Y doping (>2.0 wt.%), however, induces ZrO2 embrittlement (Figure 13d) and accelerates inward oxygen diffusion, resulting in deleterious internal oxidation layer thickening (Figure 13c) that paradoxically increases mass gain and degrades coating durability.

papers.title: Enhanced Oxidation Resistance of Ultrafine-Grain Microstructure AlCoCrFeNi High Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi HEA (ultrafine-grained, produced by stationary friction processing)
papers.approach: Microstructural refinement by friction processing at different rotational speeds followed by oxidation testing at 850–1050 °C for up to 100 h.
papers.findings: Processed samples with ultrafine grain structure show 12–48% reduction in oxidation kinetics relative to the as‐cast state. Protective oxide layers (chromia and Al‐rich inner oxides) form instead of less uniform spinels observed in unprocessed samples.
papers.mechanism: Increased grain boundary density enhances internal oxidation pathways and homogenizes composition, promoting formation of a more adherent protective oxide scale. The diffusion‐governed kinetics are modified by microstructure refinement.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding of speciated oxide growth in high entropy alloys.
papers.system: Compositionally complex HEAs under oxidizing environments (studied via in situ APT, TEM, and XRD)
papers.approach: In situ oxidation experiments at controlled temperatures (e.g., 400 °C) with APT and electron microscopy to track layered oxide formation and element-specific speciation.
papers.findings: A layered oxide structure evolves with an initial Ni-rich pre-oxide, followed by Cr-rich inner oxides and outer multi-element oxides. The preferential interactivity parameter (PIP) helps predict how different elements (e.g., Mn versus Ni/Co) segregate during oxidation.
papers.mechanism: Oxidation is governed by both thermodynamic driving forces (affinities toward oxygen) and kinetic limitations (diffusivities), leading to distinct oxide phases that may alter the mechanical performance of the HEA.

papers.title: High Temperature Oxidation Behavior of an Equimolar Cr-Mn-Fe-Co High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: Equimolar Cr-Mn-Fe-Co HEA produced by 3D laser printing
papers.approach: Isothermal oxidation experiments at 700 °C and 900 °C with mass gain measurements, XRD phase analysis, and cross-sectional microscopy.
papers.findings: At higher temperature (900 °C) oxidation produces a thick oxide scale with multiple phases (e.g., spinel, Cr2O3) and significant spallation, leading to matrix segmentation and catastrophic degradation. Oxidation kinetics follow parabolic rate laws with a rapid increase in oxide-thickness and crack formation.
papers.mechanism: Degradation is driven by rapid diffusion through nonuniform, crack-prone oxide scales that under high temperature lead to severe internal oxidation and structural disintegration.

papers.title: Mechanisms of chemical-reaction-induced tensile deformation of an Fe/Ni/Cr alloy revealed by reactive atomistic simulations.
papers.system: FCC-type Fe40Ni40Cr20 alloy used as a simplified HEA model subjected to tensile loading in vacuum and high-temperature/pressure water (oxidizing) environments
papers.approach: Atomistic uniaxial tensile simulations comparing vacuum conditions with a high-temperature/pressure water environment, focusing on dislocation generation and phase transformation.
papers.findings: In vacuum, Shockley partial dislocations lead to an FCC-to-HCP phase transformation enabling ductile deformation. In contrast, in an oxidizing environment the formation of a surface oxide layer suppresses dislocation emission, favoring an FCC-to-BCC transformation that is associated with increased brittleness and reduced ductility.
papers.mechanism: Surface oxidation alters the available deformation pathways by inhibiting conventional dislocation activity, forcing a brittle phase transition (FCC-to-BCC) that predisposes the alloy toward catastrophic failure under tensile stress.

papers.title: Effect of Post-Heat Treatment on Microstructure and Corrosion Property of Additively Manufactured AlCoCrFeNi2.1 Eutectic High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: Additively manufactured AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA (FCC+BCC phases) undergoing post-heat treatment
papers.approach: XRD investigation pre- and post-heat treatment to observe phase stability and lattice parameter changes with the aim of alleviating residual lattice distortions imparted by rapid solidification.
papers.findings: The FCC phase is dominant and its diffraction peaks shift slightly with treatment temperature indicating relief of lattice distortion. This alteration in defect levels may influence oxidation behavior indirectly.
papers.mechanism: Lattice distortion affects the local diffusion processes and thereby may modify the initiation and propagation of oxide scales.

established: Oxidation in HEAs is largely governed by the preferential oxidation of elements (Al, Cr, Mn, etc.) and follows diffusion-controlled (e.g., Wagner's parabolic law) kinetics.
Microstructural refinement (e.g., ultrafine-grained structures) can improve oxidation resistance by promoting uniform and protective oxide scales.
The formation, spallation, and composition nonuniformity of oxide scales are key drivers of degradation leading to catastrophic failure.

approaches_tried.approach: Atomistic simulations under different environmental conditions
approaches_tried.outcome: Revealed that oxidizing environments can trigger a change from ductile (FCC-to-HCP) to brittle (FCC-to-BCC) deformation mechanisms.

approaches_tried.approach: In situ APT and TEM of oxidation progression
approaches_tried.outcome: Uncovered multilayer oxide formation with distinct element segregation, helping to predict oxidation behavior via PIP parameters.

mechanisms: Diffusion-controlled oxidation leading to growth of protective (or non-protective) oxide scales.
Preferential oxidation based on elemental affinities and inter-element interactions as predicted by PIP.
Oxide-induced modification of deformation mechanisms (e.g., suppression of dislocation emission leading to brittle phase changes).
disagreements: The relative importance of specific elements (e.g., Al vs. Cr vs. Mn) in forming a protective versus a deleterious oxide layer.

open_questions: How does the presence of Ti at a lower concentration (Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3) specifically influence oxidation mechanisms compared to alloys lacking Ti or with different Al/Cr ratios?
What are the precise roles of additive manufacturing–induced microstructural defects and residual stresses on the initiation and propagation of oxide scale spallation?
How do controlled variations in the gas environment (oxidizing vs. reducing) quantitatively alter the diffusion kinetics and oxide scale composition in these HEAs?
opportunities: Investigate the effect of a controlled post-heat treatment to relieve lattice distortions (as seen in additively manufactured HEAs) on subsequent oxidation behavior, comparing oxide scale adhesion and thickness.

Combine atomistic simulations with in situ experimental methods (APT/TEM) on Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 to directly correlate oxide scale chemistry with changes in deformation mechanisms, thereby testing the FCC-to-BCC transition under oxidizing atmospheres.

Conduct systematic exposure tests under both oxidizing and reducing gas environments across a range of temperatures (e.g., 700–900 °C) to identify clear thresholds where protective oxide formation fails, offering a falsification criterion for the proposed mechanisms.

directions.direction: Manipulate the gas environment (oxidizing vs reducing) to decouple oxide composition and kinetics.
directions.assessment: Directly targets the role of environmental oxygen availability on oxide scale formation, adhesion, spallation, and ensuing internal degradation. The evidence from PMC9026100 and PMC8346963 supports that oxidation kinetics and oxide layer quality control degradation. This approach is feasible via controlled atmosphere furnaces.

directions.direction: Probe the influence of surface oxidation on deformation mechanism using atomistic simulations and in situ mechanical testing.
directions.assessment: Addresses how an oxide layer alters dislocation nucleation routes (e.g. suppressing Shockley partials) and forces an FCC-to-BCC transformation that predisposes the alloy to brittleness, as indicated in PMC9969177. It is directly relevant to uncovering why catastrophic failure occurs especially under oxidizing conditions. Combined simulation and in situ tests are challenging but informative.

directions.direction: Apply a controlled post-heat treatment to relieve residual lattice distortions from additive manufacturing.
directions.assessment: By relieving residual stresses and lattice distortions, the modified microstructure can alter diffusion paths and affect oxide scale uniformity and adhesion. Prior work (PMC12735082) suggests that post-treatment changes oxidation behavior. This intervention is practical and offers clear comparisons between treated and as-built states.

directions.direction: Introduce grain boundary engineering via surface mechanical attrition to refine microstructure.
directions.assessment: Increasing grain boundary density can promote the formation of a uniform, protective oxide scale by enhancing diffusion along boundaries and homogenizing composition, as evidenced in PMC9026100. This processing route is feasible and can yield measurable differences in oxidation kinetics and failure modes relative to as-printed samples.

directions.direction: Vary exposure duration and temperature to decouple kinetics of oxide scale growth from catastrophic failure initiation.
directions.assessment: This time‐dependent study would track how oxide thickness, composition and spallation evolve with exposure time and temperature. Although indirectly targeting the failure mechanism, it would help define precise boundaries for degradation onset and provide falsification criteria. The approach is supported by long-term oxidation tests in the literature.
